newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-MCENROE AND TARANGO ON BEST BEHAVIOUR.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-MCENROE AND TARANGO ON BEST BEHAVIOUR.

text.p: Wimbledon regulars will have recognised the soggy weather on Monday's first day but not the pair of impeccably-behaved Americans they encountered between the showers.

Who was that smiling, gracious ex-champion dressed in a sober suit and tie joking with the crowd before the official opening of the All England Club's expensive new baby, the 11,000-capacity Number One court?
And how about the model competitor on court four, wearing traditional white without a sponsor's logo in sight, politely tapping stray balls back to the ball-girls like a regular Mr Nice Guy?
Anyone with a short memory would never have guessed these were two of the most volatile characters in Wimbledon's colourful recent history, the scourge of umpires and committee-men around the world.

Certainly an identity parade in the members' enclosure would have failed to match the jovial Mr John McEnroe and the eminently respectable Mr Jeff Tarango with the descriptions on the "Most Wanted" posters in the saloon bars of Wimbledon village.
If ever there was a prodigal return to south-west London, it was McEnroe on Monday.

The man who fretted and swore his way to three Wimbledon titles between 1981 and 1984 was cheered to the recently-erected rafters of Number One court and generally behaved like a favourite uncle at a family picnic.

He swapped jokes with Boris Becker, looking every inch the successful German executive in a dark designer suit, and, having been presented with a silver salver to commemorate his past achievements, did a playful lap of honour with it balanced on his left palm like a waiter at the Ritz.
His new role as an American television commentator has clearly taught him something about the art of public relations, but Tarango's reformed behaviour has its origins in darker places.

It is two years since he left Wimbledon in disgrace, having stormed off court in his third round match against German Alexander Mronz and then accused French referee Bruno Rebeuh of being "the most corrupt official in the game" -- an allegation later withdrawn.
His wife Benedicte did not help his cause by slapping Rebeuh's face and there were no complaints from the tennis world when he was banned from last year's championships and hit with a record fine.

As recently as last month there were indications the old demons were still circling when his failure to shake hands with Thomas Muster at the end of a bad-tempered match at the French Open, followed by a rambling press conference, did little to improve his image.
It also ensured more than average interest in his first round contest with French qualifier Rodolphe Gilbert, but those who wandered over expecting an early explosion left disappointed and wet.

Heavy showers limited the action to just over two sets, in which the biggest sensation was one of the American's shoelaces coming undone. A wild forehand from Gilbert which sailed over the back netting onto the concourse further diluted any sense of unparalleled courtside drama before rain returned for the second time with Tarango trailing 6-3 5-7 1-2.
This, though, was exactly how Tarango had planned it. "They will want me to do something, but I will not see anything but the ball...it will be kind of boring," he had predicted prior to the match.

"If you check the record, I have screwed around and done weird things at other tournaments, but I had never had a fine, never had a warning, at Wimbledon until 1995. There is no way I would want to hurt the tournament."
He now admits his walk-out was a mistake but, currently lacking a clothing or racket sponsor, is clearly aware that tennis, even at Wimbledon, is no longer awash with colourful mavericks.
"I really do feel the game misses John McEnroe and needed another bad boy," he says, making a half-hearted stab at the role of misunderstood anti-hero.
The reality is that Tarango has also never remotely been in McEnroe's class as a player, and his chances of collecting the men's singles trophy on Sunday week look non-existent.
But even the slightest hint of a past reputation intrigues Wimbledon fans, which is why they slept out on the pavement all night despite the threat of rain.
McEnroe and Tarango may have let the side down, but the British weather never disappoints.
